See how he cements, and knits them together with one another, not by salutation only, but also by interchanging his Epistles. Then again he pays a compliment by addressing him individually. And this he doth not without a reason, but in order to lead the others also to emulate his zeal. For it is not a small thing not to be numbered with the rest.
16: Says that apostolic letters were read aloud and passed from church to church, so Paul tells them to read the letter from Laodicea and to pass theirs on, a letter that may be lost or may be the one we call Ephesians.
Daily Study Bible · The Mystery of the Laodicean Letter · v.16

Barclay lays out the possibilities for the missing letter: a lost letter to Laodicea, or the circular letter we know as Ephesians, which he says is the most commonly accepted answer, while noting that Paul must have written more letters than survive.

It seems to me that something was written here that the Laodiceans also needed to hear; and they, in turn, needed to learn what was written in that epistle. There is much more benefit when, from a rebuke directed against others, they learn of their own shortcomings. What then was this epistle from Laodicea? The First Epistle to Timothy: it was written from Laodicea. Some, however, say that it was an epistle that the Laodiceans were sending to Paul.
17: Reads Paul's message to Archippus, to take heed to the ministry he received in the Lord and fulfill it, as encouragement more than rebuke, delivered through the church so that he would hear it publicly.
Daily Study Bible · The Closing Blessing · vv.17–18

Barclay notes the spur to Archippus to finish the service he received from the Lord, that Paul used a secretary but signed with his own hand, and that his plea to remember his bonds carries no self-pity.

"And say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord, that thou fulfill it." Wherefore doth he not write to him? Perhaps he needed it not, but only a bare reminding, so as to be more diligent. "And say to Archippus, Take heed to the ministry which thou hast received in the Lord." His chief aim is to subject them to him entirely.
18: Notes that Paul signs in his own hand after dictating, asks them to remember his chains, and closes with grace, the only ending that suits the apostle of grace in a letter fighting a teaching of hidden mysteries and works.
Daily Study Bible · The Closing Blessing · vv.17–18

Barclay notes the spur to Archippus to finish the service he received from the Lord, that Paul used a secretary but signed with his own hand, and that his plea to remember his bonds carries no self-pity.

Remember me, who am in bonds and condemned. And the very best consolation for them is to remember Paul the prisoner in every affliction. When grace is present in you, whether you have afflictions or endure bonds, nothing of the sort will overcome you, since even being bound is a matter of grace. For Luke says: they returned from the prison, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ (cf. Acts 5:41). Do you see that to be dishonored means to be counted worthy?
